title: What Two Bank Leaders Learned From Successfully Switching Digital Banking Platforms
summary: National Exchange Bank & Trust and Tri City National Bank share how they managed digital banking platform conversion risk, data, testing, and go-live support.
body_markdown:
## Five practical lessons for banks preparing to evaluate, implement, and launch a new digital banking platform


For many[banks](https://www.alkami.com/banks/) , the hardest part of changing digital banking platforms is deciding whether or not the disruption of switching is riskier than the consequences of doing nothing.


Banks are under pressure to deliver faster, more intuitive digital experiences while managing day-to-day operations, regulatory requirements, and customer expectations. Implementing a new online banking platform may be a complex project, but staying on a platform that doesn’t meet the needs of the institution or its customers creates a different set of risks entirely.


During Alkami’s webinar[Stay or Switch? A Practical Playbook for Digital Banking Platform Decisions and Implementation](https://www.alkami.com/resources/media/webinars/stay-or-switch-a-practical-playbook-for-digital-banking-platform-decisions-and-implementation/) , Julie Stigler of[National Exchange Bank & Trust](https://nebat.com/) and Nick Bandoch of[Tri City National Bank](https://tcnb.com/) shared lessons from their own digital banking platform conversions. Their experiences point to five principles banks should consider while navigating a conversion decision.


### 1. Evaluate the cost of staying on your current digital banking platform


A digital banking platform decision should account for more than the immediate cost and complexity of implementation. Bank leaders need to consider what the current platform may be costing the institution in missed growth opportunities and ability to innovate at scale.


Tri City National Bank began evaluating new providers after concerns grew over its existing platform, including that the digital banking experience was not evolving to meet customer expectations. “I think in our case, the risk was far greater if we stayed on a platform that wasn’t evolving and wasn’t meeting customers’ needs,” Bandoch said.


National Exchange Bank & Trust faced a different situation. The bank needed to move thousands of customers to a new consumer platform while keeping its business banking platform with its incumbent provider. The bank also knew it would be one of the first financial institutions using its particular core with the Alkami Platform, which meant additional integration work. However, it also presented an opportunity for them to help pioneer how the two systems worked together within the experience.


Each conversion is unique to the needs of the organization. Banks may choose to prioritize certain platforms, customer segments, or lines of business based on their requirements and readiness. What remains consistent is the commitment to partnership and process behind every implementation.


Questions about project costs and resource requirements are always a part of the process, but bank leaders should also consider questions like:


- What customer needs are not being met today?
- Where is the current platform limiting growth or innovation?
- What risks will accumulate if the bank waits another year or two?
- Which parts of the digital experience need to change most urgently?


23% of leaders at banks and credit unions say the single biggest barrier preventing their institution from switching to a new platform provider is the overall complexity of a conversion project.


Source: Alkami Proprietary Research – 150 digital banking decision-makers. Data collected Aug 13, 2026 – Sep 10, 2026.


A clear business case should account for both sides of the decision: the short-term work of switching and the long-term cost of remaining on a platform that may hinder growth. If the project moves forward, that complexity can be managed through planning, transparency, and early preparation.


### 2. Build a cross-functional team before implementation begins


A digital banking platform implementation affects nearly every area of the bank, from IT and operations to branches, marketing, compliance, and customer support. Both banks said they involved stakeholders early in the evaluation process.


Tri City National Bank evaluated four providers with a team of approximately 12 people representing major stakeholder groups across the bank. National Exchange Bank expanded its evaluation team into a project team of about 20 people, including representatives from operations, deposits, lending, IT, compliance, marketing, and other teams. This broader involvement helped each bank surface questions and requirements that might not have been identified by a smaller digital banking or IT team.


Bandoch described the process as an opportunity to build commitment rather than seek unanimous consensus. Not everyone needed to prefer the same provider, but everyone needed the opportunity to ask questions, meet the vendors, and understand the decision before implementation began.


Stigler emphasized the importance of transparency and regular communication. National Exchange Bank’s project team met weekly, and team members shared updates with their individual departments so there was a consistent flow of information across the organization and employees understood what was changing and why.


### 3. Prepare data, integrations, and processes before the project demands them


Preparation is one of the most important ways banks can reduce digital banking platform conversion risk. It is also an area where oversight can create significant work later in the project.


Bandoch identified data cleanup as one area Tri City National Bank underestimated. Customer phone numbers, for example, were not always stored consistently across primary, secondary, and mobile fields. The bank also completed a major deposit product cleanup before implementation. It reduced more than 80 miscellaneous deposit products to approximately 35, making product mapping and configuration more manageable when it came time to conversion.


Stigler shared a related lesson about integrations and process discovery. “Be specific in your questions and responses about integrations and processes. Go down to the minutiae and explain,” she said.


A simple integration discussion may not reveal every custom tool, workflow, or legacy process that employees and customers rely on. Stigler described how a custom international bill-pay capability could easily have been overlooked if the bank had not reviewed its existing platform in detail. Clean data and detailed requirements ensure that the new platform works as expected and accounts for the needs of the bank.


Before implementation begins, banks should document every:


- Integration
- Custom workflow
- Account and deposit product
- Customer-facing process
- Internal team that depends on the platform
- Exception or manual workaround


Both banks found that Alkami’s implementation team’s approach to solution design was an important part of internal readiness. By reviewing the current platform in detail and configuring a test environment that reflects the bank’s future-state experience, teams were able to identify gaps before formal testing begins and reduce risk. Instead of discovering an overlooked capability late in the project, the bank can address it months earlier, before it creates launch delays or customer-impacting issues.


### 4. Treat go-live as a coordinated customer experience initiative


Banks focus on marketing and sending multiple communications through a number of channels prior to launch, but go-live is the moment when customers experience the quality of the bank’s preparation. It is also when the bank’s internal teams, technology providers, core provider, and third-party vendors must work together under pressure.


For Tri City National Bank, launch coordination included the primary customer care team, branch employees, other departments across the bank, Alkami, and core representatives. Bandoch said having everyone in the same room made it easier to hear issues directly from customers and employees, identify patterns, and resolve problems.


Tri City National Bank also created a concierge support model for approximately 300 commercial customers. About 20 bankers each supported a group of customers and provided direct points of contact during the transition. A separate triage team supported those bankers when issues arose.


National Exchange Bank used several additional strategies to support customers and employees, including having digital banking champions at each branch and dedicated phone and email support. As Stigler explained, “They are actually still the first line of defense. So customers, if they have questions in regards to their online banking, they actually typically speak with our champions before they get back to our digital banking team.”


Aside from migrating customers to a new platform, go-live should be treated as an opportunity to help customers successfully adopt the new system. A launch plan should be designed around the questions customers will have and how it will improve their banking experience.


### 5. Overcommunicate, monitor adoption, and lead with empathy after launch


Both banks monitored adoption rates closely after launch while helping employees and customers adjust. Tri City National Bank also tracked call volume and wait times, reviewed App Store feedback, and monitored account and deposit activity in the weeks that followed. National Exchange Bank shared adoption progress with the project team and the selected branch-based banking champions. As adoption increased, the data became a source of momentum and encouragement for employees.


Post-launch questions often come down to helping customers access the platform, enroll a device, navigate a new workflow, or understand what is different, which is where empathy comes in. Customers did not choose the conversion, and employees may also be learning the new experience while supporting them. Acknowledging frustration before trying to solve the problem can make the interaction more productive and help preserve trust.


Banks should prepare to:


- Expect a significant increase in call volume during the first week.
- Test phone systems before launch to ensure they can handle a surge in calls.
- Make digital banking support easy to find in call routing, online, and in-branch.
- Prepare teams to troubleshoot devices, browsers, and enrollment issues.
- Monitor adoption, call volume, wait times, and common support issues.
- Keep communication open among the bank, platform provider, core provider, and third-party vendors.
- Recognize employees for the additional work required during launch.


Both leaders also highlighted the importance of planning for employee fatigue. The weekend before launch can involve long hours and intensive file conversion work, often immediately before the busiest week of the project. Staffing, food, breaks, morale initiatives, and backup resources should all be part of the launch plan.


The experiences of National Exchange Bank & Trust and Tri City National Bank show that successful digital banking platform conversions depend on many factors, from thorough data and integration preparation to empathetic communication. Knowing the positive impact a digital banking conversion would have on their customers’ and employees’ experiences deemed the time-intensive project to be worth it. With the promise of innovation on the horizon, the banks’ behind-the-scenes work helped ensure a smooth transition and set them up to continue building deeper relationships with customers long after go-live.

### Successful conversion starts with internal readiness


There is no perfect implementation project. Even well-planned conversions will include unexpected questions, exceptions, and moments that require teams to adapt.

### FAQs


1


How can banks reduce risk during a digital banking platform conversion?


Banks can reduce conversion risk by preparing early. That includes cleaning customer and product data, documenting integrations and custom processes, involving the right stakeholders, and testing in an environment that reflects the institution’s future-state configuration. Early preparation helps teams identify gaps before they affect the launch timeline or customer experience.


2


How can banks prepare employees and customers for digital banking go-live?


Banks should communicate early and often, train employees on the new experience, involve staff in testing, and prepare dedicated support resources for launch. Banking champions, expanded call-center coverage, branch support, and clear escalation processes can help customers get assistance when they need it.


3


How can banks measure the success of a digital banking platform conversion?


Banks can monitor adoption rates, call volume, wait times, common support issues, customer feedback, and account activity after launch. These measures can help identify where customers need additional support, evaluate business continuity, and determine whether the new platform is delivering the intended experience.
